docs.title: The Sum Function in C++
docs.text:
Author(s):

(RGB) Raghav B. Venkataramaiyer <bv.raghav -at- thapar -dot- edu>

This project creates a sum function in c++ as a sample to illustrate how to compile a shared library and distribute it for use along with the binary.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
make -C code

This will create create a folder dist in code folder, with following contents

dist
 +-lib
 |  \-libbvr_math.so
 +-bin
    \-run

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
cd code
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=dist/lib
./dist/bin/run

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Render deployment runbook
docs.text: This runbook deploys the existing BloodLine static frontend and FastAPI API as separate Render services. The database can be hosted by Neon; a Render-managed PostgreSQL database is optional. It does not replace the GitHub Pages documentation workflow. Deploy only after reviewing the source and setting private secrets in Render.

docs.title: Recommended services
docs.text:
Service Render type Repository settings Persistent data Frontend Static Site Root directory code/frontend; build command python build_static.py; publish directory dist None API Docker Web Service Root directory code/backend; Dockerfile path Dockerfile; health check /health Managed database only Database PostgreSQL (Neon or another provider) Set the provider's PostgreSQL URL as DATABASE_URL; Neon requires TLS Provider-managed database

The frontend does not run inside FastAPI. Its static build injects the public API origin into config.js; no API secret is placed in the frontend bundle. The API container applies Alembic migrations at startup and binds Uvicorn to 0.0.0.0:$PORT (fallback 8000 for local Docker).

docs.title: Create and configure services
docs.text:
1. Create a PostgreSQL database with your chosen provider. For Neon, copy its direct (non-pooler) PostgreSQL URL from the Neon Console and keep sslmode=require (and any supplied channel_binding=require) in the query string. Neon URLs in the standard postgresql://user:password@host/database?sslmode=require form are supported by SQLAlchemy and the installed psycopg2-binary driver; the same URL is used by the app and Alembic. Store it only in Render's private DATABASE_URL environment variable. A Render-managed database is optional; if you choose one, use its internal URL and select a plan whose persistence and retention meet your needs.
  2. Create a Docker Web Service connected to this repository, branch master, root directory code/backend, Dockerfile Dockerfile, health check path /health. Do not set a separate start command; the image command runs migrations then Uvicorn. Render supplies PORT.
  3. Add these API environment variables in Render (not in Git):
Name Value DATABASE_URL Secret PostgreSQL URL from Neon or another provider (for Neon, use the direct URL with TLS enabled) BLOODLINE_ENV production BLOODLINE_USE_MIGRATIONS 1 BLOODLINE_SECRET_KEY Unique random secret, generated privately (for example python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))') BLOODLINE_DEMO_LOGIN 0 BLOODLINE_DEMO_TOOLS 0 BLOODLINE_FACULTY_DEMO 1 only when enabling the synthetic faculty demo ALLOWED_ORIGINS Exact HTTPS origin of the Render static site, with no path or trailing slash

Optional: set BLOODLINE_SARIMA=0 if you prefer to disable SARIMA. VAPID values are needed only if you plan to enable web push. Do not set or reuse the development JWT secret. 4. Create a Render Static Site from the same repo and branch. Set root directory code/frontend, build command python build_static.py, and publish directory dist. Set BLOODLINE_API_URL to the API's exact public HTTPS origin (for example https://bloodline-api.onrender.com, no path, query, or credentials). The build rejects invalid, local, credential-bearing, and non-HTTPS URLs. Set BLOODLINE_FACULTY_DEMO=1 in the Static Site build environment only when enabling the original synthetic account shortcuts; otherwise use 0. 5. Once the static site exists, copy its exact origin (scheme + host, no path) into API ALLOWED_ORIGINS. Save both services and wait for their builds. 6. Confirm https://<api-host>/health, then https://<api-host>/docs; check the static site's browser network panel for successful API calls and CORS responses.

docs.title: One-time safe database bootstrap
docs.text:
The image's startup command runs Alembic migrations only; migrations intentionally do not create an administrator or sample records. After the API is running and migrations have completed:

  1. Run bootstrap from a trusted machine with the backend dependencies installed and network access to the database, setting DATABASE_URL, BLOODLINE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAIL, and a unique BLOODLINE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD (16-72 UTF-8 bytes) in that machine's private environment. Do not put the password in a command argument or repository file. Render Free Web Services do not provide a Shell, so this local one-time step also works when using Render Free compute.
  2. From code/backend, run python -m app.bootstrap. It additively creates missing roles, the initial system administrator if that email does not already exist, three explicitly synthetic planning regions, stock snapshots, and 180 days of synthetic demand per region and blood group. It creates no donors or patients, never changes existing stock/accounts/history, and can be rerun safely.
  3. Unset BLOODLINE_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD from the trusted machine's environment as soon as the command completes; do not add it to the Render service environment. Keep the admin email if useful for audit; rotate the initial password through normal account administration if required.
  4. Sign in as the administrator, create individual staff accounts, and verify role-specific navigation and dashboards. Donors can register through the public donor registration form.

docs.title: Optional original faculty demo fixture
docs.text:
The original demo picker is separate from the real administrator login. To enable it, set BLOODLINE_FACULTY_DEMO=1 on both the API and Static Site, keep BLOODLINE_DEMO_LOGIN=0 and BLOODLINE_DEMO_TOOLS=0, and deploy the additive demo-scope migration. After reviewing 0002_demo_scope.py and app.bootstrap_demo, run python -m app.bootstrap_demo once with the private production DATABASE_URL. This creates only the original five non-donor accounts and fifteen synthetic donors, plus synthetic demo banks, inventory, demand, requests, and screening fixtures. It refuses to take over any reserved email already belonging to a non-demo account and never changes the real administrator. Reruns add only missing records. The historical shared demo password and unauthenticated direct login are not restored; the visible shortcuts use a rate-limited short-lived demo token. Demo Admin is read-only for demo records; all other demo activity is scoped to synthetic records. Demo outreach sends push notifications to browsers that enabled them on a demo donor account. Do not run the destructive app.seed against this database.

Never run python -m app.seed against a production database: it drops mapped tables. It now refuses BLOODLINE_ENV=production, non-SQLite database URLs, and runs without explicit BLOODLINE_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_SEED=1; bootstrap does not call that script. Do not load real donor or patient information into this academic prototype.

docs.title: Persistence and operations
docs.text:
Keep the API container filesystem out of persistent data storage. Do not point production at SQLite or a container-local file. Configure backups/retention available on the selected database plan. DATABASE_URL should be kept private. Render Free Web Services can make outbound PostgreSQL connections to an external provider such as Neon; this uses public internet bandwidth and is subject to Render's free-service limits. It does not require a Render Postgres service. Render Free Web Services sleep after inactivity and are intended for preview/hobby use, not durable production workloads.

The frontend origin must match ALLOWED_ORIGINS exactly. If you add a custom domain or preview frontend, add only its exact HTTPS origin to that variable and rebuild the static frontend if its API URL changes. Login throttling is process-local, so it is not shared across API instances; use a single API instance for this prototype and consider shared rate limiting before scaling.

docs.title: Important limitations
docs.text: BloodLine uses synthetic demand, has no operational clinical validation, and should not be used for actual allocation or medical decisions. Render service pricing and free-tier limits can change; check the provider's current pricing and persistence terms before selecting a plan.

docs.title: BloodLine — Predictive Blood Shortage & Smart Donor Matching Platform
docs.text: Inventory tracking, 7-day demand forecasting, rule-based shortage-risk detection and donor matching in one role-based web app (FastAPI + SQLAlchemy backend, dependency-free static frontend). All demand data is synthetic/simulated and labelled as such. BloodLine never makes medical eligibility decisions: donors are only suggested, and medical staff enter every screening outcome.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text: No build step and no npm packages (works offline): frontend/index.html (app), frontend/viz.js (hand-built SVG visual kit: liquid blood-drop tiles, tick gauges, donut, interactive area/bar charts with tooltips, count-up numbers) and frontend/sw.js (Web Push). Dark and light themes, saved per browser, following the system setting on first visit. Respects prefers-reduced-motion.

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
cd backend
python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate     # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
BLOODLINE_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE_SEED=1 python -m app.seed # disposable SQLite only; drops tables and prompts for a local password
uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000             # docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

cd ../frontend && python3 -m http.server 5500         # open http://localhost:5500
The frontend calls http://localhost:8000; to change it run localStorage.bl_api = "https://your-api" in the browser console. The login page lists every demo account (staff chips plus a picker for all 15 donors with blood group and status). Historical demo logins (the former shared password was retired; the seed command now prompts for a local-only password): manager@, inventory@, hospital@, screening@, admin@, donor1@ … donor15@ bloodline.demo.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Purpose Default DATABASE_URL SQLAlchemy URL (SQLite or PostgreSQL) sqlite:///./bloodline.db BLOODLINE_SECRET_KEY JWT signing key (required when BLOODLINE_ENV=production) dev placeholder BLOODLINE_ENV production refuses to start with the placeholder secret unset ALLOWED_ORIGINS comma-separated CORS origins * BLOODLINE_SARIMA set 0 to disable the SARIMA candidate (baseline + exponential smoothing only) enabled BLOODLINE_USE_MIGRATIONS 1 = schema managed by Alembic instead of create_all unset BLOODLINE_SHELF_<COMPONENT> shelf life in days, e.g. BLOODLINE_SHELF_PLATELETS=5 (defaults are planning values, not medical guidance: set your blood centre's policy) whole_blood 35, red_cells 42, platelets 5, plasma 365 BLOODLINE_DEMO_TOOLS 0 disables POST /demo/scenario (the Scenarios page's simulate-shortage/restock buttons, which change stock); always off in production enabled LOGIN_RATE_LIMIT 0 turns login rate limiting off on LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS / LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS_PER_IP / LOGIN_WINDOW_SECONDS failed sign-ins allowed per account+IP / per IP within the window (then HTTP 429 with Retry-After) 5 / 20 / 900 BLOODLINE_DEMO_LOGIN 0 disables GET /auth/demo-accounts (the unauthenticated demo account picker on the login page); always off when BLOODLINE_ENV=production enabled VAPID_PUBLIC_KEY / VAPID_PRIVATE_KEY / VAPID_SUBJECT enable Web Push (generate with python scripts/gen_vapid.py) push disabled

docs.title: Forecasting notes
docs.text: SARIMA needs statsmodels (in requirements.txt); if it is missing or a fit fails, the pipeline falls back to the other two models without error. It needs at least 60 days of history. Fitting takes a moment, so results are cached while the data is unchanged: the first dashboard load after seeding can be slower than later ones. Forecasts are trained on synthetic data and are risk signals, not validated clinical predictions.

docs.title: Tests, lint, CI
docs.text:
cd backend && pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
ruff check . && pytest -q       # tests/test_logic.py (pure logic) + tests/test_api.py (end-to-end, temp DB)
GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs lint + tests and builds the API image on every push.

docs.title: Docker / PostgreSQL
docs.text:
cp .env.example .env            # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD and BLOODLINE_SECRET_KEY
docker compose up --build       # API :8000, web :8080, PostgreSQL
docker compose exec api python -m app.seed

docs.title: SRS coverage
docs.text:
Implemented: AUTH-1..4 · INV-1..6 (donation recording requires an 'eligible' screening; single units with collection/expiry dates, oldest issued first, expiry panel) · FCST-1..4 (moving-average baseline vs exponential smoothing vs SARIMA(1,0,1)(1,0,1,7), one chronological one-step-ahead backtest, MAE + RMSE, lowest MAE selected) · RISK-1..3 (alerts stored, de-duplicated, with history) · MATCH-1..5 (incl. optional radius) · REQ-1/2 · SCR-1 · NOTE-1 (in-app plus optional Web Push, sent only to donors who pass the matching rules) · RPT-1 (CSV and browser print-to-PDF) · REG-1 (multi-bank stock/risk heatmap, bank map, redistribution suggestions that always require human approval) · DON-1 · ADM-1/2 · Alembic migrations · CI + staging CD workflow.

Also included: Evaluation page (/evaluation/report: forecast MAE/RMSE per blood group, shortage-detection precision/recall/F1 on a chronological protocol, independent SRS rule check of donor matching and notification targeting, browser-measured response times) · Scenarios page (read-only what-if demand slider; demo-only simulate-shortage/restock, recorded as simulated) · login rate limiting (in memory: resets on restart and isn't shared across workers; behind a proxy all clients share its IP) · Cmd/Ctrl+K command palette.

Deliberately not implemented: * Prophet. FR-FCST-2 asks for "Prophet or SARIMA"; SARIMA is in. Prophet needs a heavy Stan toolchain and can't be scored with the same frozen-parameter one-step-ahead protocol, so a side-by-side comparison would not be fair. services/forecasting.py is modular if you want to add it as another candidate. * Google Maps. The regional view uses a dependency-free SVG; a maps API needs a key and billing account. * Server-side PDF. PDF export uses the browser's print-to-PDF with a print stylesheet (no extra dependency).

Needs your setup (untested here): Web Push (VAPID keys + HTTPS or localhost), the staging deploy (needs a server and the secrets listed in .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml; without them it only publishes the image to GitHub Container Registry), PostgreSQL via Docker.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
cd backend && alembic upgrade head          # new database
alembic stamp head                          # existing database already created by app.seed / create_all
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "describe change"   # future schema changes
0001_baseline builds the 1.0 schema with create_all; replace it with an explicit autogenerated baseline before your next model change (instructions are in the file).

docs.title: Changes made to the earlier prototype
docs.text:
• /risk/{bank} stored a new alert on every page load; it now de-duplicates and has /risk/{bank}/history.
  • A screening outcome of "eligible" used to overwrite last_donation_date; it is now set only when a donation is recorded.
  • Matching showed "999 days since last donation" for first-time donors; it now says "No donation on record".
  • Forecast responses now include MAE/RMSE; matching returns distance_km.
  • Synthetic demand data changed on every seed run because Python randomises hash() per process; it now uses a stable checksum, so seeded data is reproducible.
  • frontend/legacy-index.html is a retained, unused legacy UI. It is not linked from the active frontend or included in the Render static build; it is preserved for reference and is not maintained.

docs.title: Earlier prototype notes (W6/W7)
docs.text:
Predictive blood shortage & smart donor matching platform.

This is the first working prototype, built directly on top of the W5 vertical slice (nothing from W5 was rewritten — inventory, demand generation, forecasting, shortage-risk, and donor matching all work exactly as before). W6 added the remaining role workflows, an integrated hospital request → approval → inventory-issue flow, and a proper UI shell so the whole thing reads as one coherent product rather than a handful of pages.

docs.title: 1. Setup
docs.text:
cd backend
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate        # Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: 2. Seed demo data
docs.text:
python -m app.seed

This creates one blood bank, seeded inventory (some blood groups deliberately low to demonstrate HIGH risk), 180 days of synthetic demand history per blood group, 15 donor records, one hospital with three sample blood requests (mixed statuses), one sample screening record, and one demo account per role — see credentials below.

docs.title: 3. Run the backend
docs.text:
uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000
API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

docs.title: 4. Run the frontend
docs.text:
Still a single static HTML file, no build step (see frontend/index.html) — deliberately kept off React for the prototype so there's zero toolchain to break during a live demo. Swapping to React/Vite later only touches this file; the API contract is unaffected either way.

cd ../frontend
python3 -m http.server 5500
Open http://localhost:5500

docs.title: 5. Demo credentials
docs.text:
The former shared demo password has been retired; the current local seed prompts for a password and is restricted to explicitly opted-in SQLite development databases.

Role Email Blood Bank Manager manager@bloodline.demo Inventory Staff inventory@bloodline.demo Hospital Coordinator hospital@bloodline.demo Medical / Screening Staff screening@bloodline.demo System Admin admin@bloodline.demo Donor (×15) donor1@bloodline.demo … donor15@bloodline.demo

docs.title: 6. W7 demo sequence
docs.text:
1. Log in as Manager → Overview shows total stock, high-risk count, pending requests, and a critical-shortages panel with an inline "Find donors" action.
  2. Open Inventory → current stock per blood group.
  3. Open Demand History → pick a blood group, see the 180-day synthetic series (chart + table + summary stats), clearly labelled synthetic.
  4. Open Shortage Risk → HIGH/MODERATE/LOW per group with the plain- English shortfall explanation, and "Find donors" on any at-risk group.
  5. Open Blood Requests → see the pending queue.
  6. Log out, log in as Hospital Coordinator → submit a new B+ request (urgent/emergency), see it appear with status pending.
  7. Log out, log in as Manager → Blood Requests → Approve the new request. If stock covers it, inventory is auto-issued and status becomes fulfilled; watch the number actually drop.
  8. Log out, log in as Inventory Staff → manually record a receipt/issue and watch the grid update immediately, with proper validation (no negative units, can't issue more than available).
  9. Optionally also show: - Reports (manager) — received/issued/expired totals, risk summary, demand-vs-forecast table. - Screening (medical staff) — candidate donor worklist, record an eligible/deferred/rejected outcome. - My Profile (donor) — eligibility status, donation history, availability/consent toggle. - Admin — user counts by role, full user list.

docs.title: 7. What changed in the W7 polish pass (on top of W6)
docs.text:
Real bug fixed: "Find donors" from the Manager Overview page silently did nothing useful — the results container was being dropped from the DOM by a templating helper that only kept the first of two sibling elements it built. Root cause fixed by rebuilding that section with the same single-string innerHTML pattern the (working) Shortage Risk page already used, and both pages now share one findDonorsInto() function so there's one code path instead of two that can drift apart again.

Screening workflow rebuilt: "Screen" now opens a modal showing the donor's blood group, availability, cooldown status, and last donation before recording an outcome. Submitting reloads the whole candidate table from the API (not just closes a form), so the new outcome and screening date are visibly persisted without a manual refresh. Added a "Last screened" column, backed by a new last_screened_at field.

Login page redesigned: subtitle added, demo credentials moved behind a "For demonstration" toggle instead of being printed on the page by default, per-account quick-fill buttons inside the toggle.

Inventory Staff dashboard extended: now shows a low-stock indicator on tiles under 15 units, and a Recent Transactions feed (new endpoint, GET /inventory/transactions) — without duplicating the manager's forecast-based risk view.

Reports page extended: added Blood Group Distribution and Blood Requests Summary sections (new inventory_by_group / requests_summary fields on the existing endpoint).

UI alignment/responsiveness: sidebar is now sticky and full-height, tables scroll horizontally on narrow screens instead of overflowing, badges and long text no longer break card layouts, and a single .shortage-row style is now shared everywhere a HIGH/MODERATE shortage row is rendered.

Manager approve/reject now show inline success/error messages in the page instead of a browser alert() popup.

New backend endpoint: GET /inventory/transactions (recent stock movements, newest first).

docs.title: 8. What changed in W6 — file by file
docs.text:
Schema: one additive column, BloodRequest.notes (nullable). Nothing else in the 19-table schema changed shape.

New backend routers (all reuse the existing services — forecasting, risk, donor matching — nothing was duplicated): - routers/hospital.py — hospital coordinator creates/views own requests - routers/requests.py — manager reviews pending requests; approve auto-issues inventory via the same transaction logic inventory.py already used, demonstrating the request → approval → inventory flow end-to-end - routers/screening.py — candidate worklist + record screening outcome - routers/admin.py — system-wide counts + user list - routers/donor.py — donor's own profile, donation history, availability - routers/reports.py — aggregates existing inventory transactions + reruns the existing forecast/risk functions per group

Fixed: inventory.py now rejects zero/negative transaction quantities (the one genuine validation gap from W5).

Frontend: full restyle — sidebar navigation, card-based dashboards, consistent badges (blood group / risk level / status), clean tables, and a page per role — still one HTML file, still vanilla JS, still calling the same API. No page was invented without a backing endpoint.

Seed data: added a hospital + hospital coordinator, an admin account, a medical-staff account, three sample blood requests, and one sample screening record, so no role's first login shows an empty page.

docs.title: 9. What's intentionally left for W8+ / second prototype
docs.text:
• Prophet/SARIMA forecasting (the proposal explicitly scopes this later — the current model is naive-baseline vs. exponential smoothing, honestly labelled as such in the API response)
  • Targeted donor push notifications (schema exists — DonorNotification — unused until this phase)
  • Regional multi-bank surplus/redistribution view
  • Managed/production deployment, PostgreSQL migration, CI/CD hardening
  • Fine-grained donor availability windows (DonorAvailability table exists, unused — donor availability is currently a simple on/off toggle)
  • Saved/exported PDF reports (Report table exists, unused — the current Reports page is live-computed, not persisted)

docs.title: 10. Likely professor questions
docs.text:
"Is this forecast really Prophet/SARIMA?" No — deliberately not yet. It's naive-baseline vs. exponential smoothing, and the API always reports which one it picked and why (backtested MAE). Prophet/SARIMA is explicit W8+ scope per the proposal; the forecasting module is structured so swapping the model doesn't change the API contract.

"Is the demand data real?" No, and the UI says so on every page that shows it — "Synthetic / Simulated Demand Data" — because the prototype has no access to granular real blood-bank consumption data. The generation method (baseline + weekly pattern + seasonal effect + holiday bump + emergency spike + noise) is documented in services/synthetic_data.py and explained in-app.

"Does approving a request actually do anything, or is it just a status flag?" It actually issues inventory — same InventoryTransaction mechanism the Inventory Staff page uses — so the stock number visibly drops. If stock is insufficient it stays pending with a note rather than silently failing.

"Why is the frontend vanilla JS and not React, when the proposal says React?" Speed and reliability for a first prototype: no build step to break during a demo. The API is framework-agnostic — swapping in the React+Tailwind frontend from the proposal is a frontend-only change later.

"What decides donor eligibility — the system or a person?" A person. Screening records an outcome a human medical staff member entered; BloodLine never auto-approves a donor. This is enforced at the data-model level (ScreeningRecord.performed_by_id requires a Staff row) not just a UI convention.

docs.title: 11. Swapping SQLite → PostgreSQL
docs.text:
export DATABASE_URL="postgresql+psycopg2://user:pass@localhost:5432/bloodline"
pip install psycopg2-binary
No model or route code changes needed.

docs.title: UCS503P Project Template
docs.text:
This is a project template for UCS503P Project (2026-27 ODD).

There are 3 reports in LaTeX format, namely a) Project Proposal, b) Project Report Prototype Stage, and c) Project Report Final -- each in their respective folders.

Journals are stacked under the folder journals, one folder for each team member. A sample entry has been made for example.

The source code is contained within the folder code.

The documentation is under folder docs.

All other aspects of code organisation are left to the discretion of the user(s).

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
As of now, the docs is just an organised collection of markdown (md) files. But the build procedure is using mkdocs backend. As a result, any commit into the master branch of github repository would result in CI/CD based build and deployment of the documentation including the journals.

For a local DEV-version of the docs for viewing and testing, install the local env and issue the following command:

make docs

docs.title: BloodLine screenshots
docs.text:
These PNGs are genuine captures from a local run of the application using its seeded synthetic data. They were taken with headless Chrome at a 1600 × 1100 viewport. The matching interfaces and forecast results were allowed to render before capture.

  • login.png — signed-out page
  • dashboard.png — manager Overview after sign-in
  • inventory.png — Inventory page
  • forecasting.png — Forecast page after running a forecast

Objective

docs.text:
• Deployed the application on Render's free tier: the frontend as a static site and the FastAPI backend as a Docker web service, with a Neon PostgreSQL database. Pushes to master redeploy both services automatically.

  • Made the one-click demo logins persist: when demo mode is enabled the API adds any missing synthetic demo accounts on every start, and the login page detects demo mode from the API.
  • Found that the dashboard stayed blank for more than 90 seconds on the live server because fitting SARIMA was too slow for the free CPU. The SARIMA code fitted each series twice (once before the holdout for the backtest and once on the full history for the forecast); it now fits once and continues the forecast from the same fitted model, which made it about 20 times faster (18.7 s to 0.9 s for O+ locally) with the same backtest errors. The API also fits SARIMA for every bank and blood group in the background after it starts, so the Forecast, Shortage risk, Regional and Evaluation pages all compare SARIMA and load in a few seconds. On the live data SARIMA has the lowest MAE for all eight blood groups.
  • Added a "Waking up the server" message, shown when the free server is starting after a period of inactivity, instead of a blank page.

docs.title: Problems and Fixes
docs.text:

  • Wrong notification times: server times are stored in UTC without a time-zone marker; the frontend now treats them as UTC.
  • No O+ donors in the demo: the only O+ demo donor was in cooldown; the demo setup now keeps one donor per group available.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To generate realistic synthetic blood-demand data for developing and testing the forecasting module.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Detailed real-world blood-bank demand data was not available for the prototype. Therefore, synthetic data was required to simulate historical blood demand.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented synthetic demand generation.
  • Generated 180 days of historical demand.
  • Generated demand for all eight blood groups.
  • Defined different baseline demand levels for each blood group.
  • Added weekly demand patterns.
  • Added seasonal variation.
  • Added holiday/event effects.
  • Added rare emergency spikes.
  • Added random noise to make the data more realistic.
  • Ensured that generated demand values remain non-negative.

docs.title: Demand Model
docs.text:
The generated demand is based on multiple components:

Demand =
Baseline
+ Weekly Pattern
+ Seasonal Effect
+ Holiday Bump
+ Emergency Spike
+ Random Noise

docs.title: Parameters Used
docs.text:
Component Value Baseline (units/day) O+ 18, A+ 15, B+ 13, O- 7, A- 6, AB+ 5, B- 5, AB- 2.5 (higher for common blood groups) Weekly pattern +10% of baseline on weekdays, -18% on weekends (elective surgery is scheduled midweek) Seasonal effect Yearly sine wave with an amplitude of 12% of baseline Holiday bump +35% of baseline within two days of eight fixed days of the year (festival/accident periods) Emergency spike On about 2% of days, an extra 80-180% of baseline (mass-casualty or local emergencies) Random noise Gaussian noise with a standard deviation of 8% of baseline

Final values are clipped at zero and rounded to one decimal place. Each blood group uses a fixed random seed derived from its name, so the same data is generated on every run and results can be reproduced.

docs.title: Labelling
docs.text: The data is stored with an is_synthetic flag and every page and API response that shows it labels it as synthetic, so it is never presented as real hospital statistics.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text: A forecasting model can only be tested properly if the data contains realistic structure. Combining a per-group baseline with weekly, seasonal and random components produces data that behaves like real demand, including occasional unpredictable spikes that the models must cope with.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A reproducible 180-day synthetic demand dataset for all eight blood groups was created and used to develop and evaluate the forecasting and shortage-risk components.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To implement short-term blood-demand forecasting using simple and interpretable forecasting techniques.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Studied time-series demand forecasting.
  • Implemented a 14-day baseline forecasting method.
  • Implemented Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES).
  • Used an alpha value of 0.3 for SES.
  • Generated forecasts for the next 7 days.
  • Integrated the forecasting logic into the backend service.

docs.title: 14-Day Baseline
docs.text:
The baseline uses the recent 14 days of observed demand to estimate the current daily demand level.

Baseline = Average demand over the last 14 days

The 14-day period is the historical look-back window, while the 7-day period is the future forecast horizon.

docs.title: Simple Exponential Smoothing
docs.text:
SES gives more importance to recent observations while gradually reducing the influence of older observations.

The smoothing equation is:

L_t = αX_t + (1 - α)L_(t-1)

where:

α = 0.3

docs.title: Forecast Horizon
docs.text: The system generates a short-term forecast for the next 7 days.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text:
The historical look-back period and forecast horizon have different purposes:

  • 14 days → data used to estimate the current demand level
  • 7 days → period for which demand is predicted

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The demand forecasting component was implemented and connected to the BloodLine backend.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To evaluate the forecasting approaches and select the better-performing model using historical data.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: A forecasting model should be evaluated before being used for future predictions. Since actual future demand is not available at the time of forecasting, historical data was used for backtesting.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented rolling-origin backtesting.
  • Evaluated both the baseline and SES forecasting approaches.
  • Used Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as the evaluation metric.
  • Compared predicted historical demand with actual historical demand.
  • Calculated the error for different forecasting origins.
  • Compared the average MAE of the candidate models.
  • Selected the model with the lower MAE.

docs.title: Backtesting Process
docs.text: Historical Demand ↓ Select a historical forecast origin ↓ Generate forecast using only previous data ↓ Compare forecast with actual demand ↓ Calculate MAE ↓ Move the forecast origin forward ↓ Repeat

docs.title: MAE
docs.text:
Mean Absolute Error is calculated as:

MAE = Mean(|Actual - Predicted|)

A lower MAE indicates that the forecasting method produced smaller prediction errors.

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text: The baseline and SES models were evaluated using the same historical data. The model producing the lower MAE was selected for the final forecast.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text: The actual future demand cannot be compared with today's prediction immediately because the future values are not yet known. Backtesting solves this problem by using known historical data to simulate future predictions.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The forecasting pipeline was enhanced with objective evaluation and model selection instead of relying on a single forecasting method without validation.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To determine whether the predicted blood demand can be met using the current inventory and classify the shortage risk.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Implemented shortage-risk detection.
  • Used forecasted demand and current stock as inputs.
  • Calculated the expected shortfall.
  • Implemented LOW, MODERATE, and HIGH risk levels.
  • Added special handling for zero-stock situations.
  • Generated explanations for the assigned risk level.

docs.title: Shortfall Calculation
docs.text:
The expected shortage is calculated as:

Shortfall = Predicted Demand - Current Stock

For example:

Predicted demand = 83.4 units Current stock = 10 units

Shortfall = 83.4 - 10 = 73.4 units

docs.title: LOW
docs.text:
Shortfall ≤ 0

The current stock is sufficient to cover the predicted demand.

docs.title: MODERATE
docs.text:
0 < Shortfall ≤ 25% of current stock

There is a shortage, but it remains within the defined moderate threshold.

docs.title: HIGH
docs.text:
Shortfall > 25% of current stock

A zero-stock situation with positive predicted demand is also treated as HIGH risk.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Current stock = 10 7-day forecast = 83.4

Shortfall = 83.4 - 10 = 73.4

Since the shortfall is greater than the defined threshold, the blood group is classified as HIGH risk.

docs.title: Key Learning
docs.text: Forecasting tells us how much blood may be required, while shortage-risk detection determines whether the current inventory is sufficient to satisfy that predicted demand.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A rule-based shortage-risk detection layer was implemented on top of the forecasting output, producing interpretable LOW, MODERATE, and HIGH risk levels.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To integrate the forecasting and shortage-risk components with the BloodLine application and verify their complete workflow.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Integrated the forecasting service with the BloodLine backend.
  • Integrated shortage-risk calculations with the application.
  • Connected forecasting and risk results with the dashboard.
  • Verified that forecasted demand and shortage-risk levels are displayed for blood groups.
  • Tested different inventory and demand scenarios.
  • Verified LOW, MODERATE, and HIGH risk classification.
  • Tested the complete flow from historical demand to forecast and risk detection.
  • Verified that high-risk results can lead to the donor-matching workflow.

docs.title: End-to-End Workflow
docs.text: Historical Demand ↓ Demand Forecasting ↓ Baseline / SES Evaluation ↓ Selected Forecast ↓ Compare Forecast with Current Stock ↓ Shortfall Calculation ↓ Risk Classification ↓ LOW / MODERATE / HIGH ↓ Dashboard / Risk Alert ↓ Potential Donor Matching

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The predictive workflow was tested using different combinations of:

  • Blood groups
  • Current inventory levels
  • Forecasted demand
  • Shortage conditions
  • Zero-stock situations

The results were checked to ensure that the calculated risk level matched the defined rules.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: The demand forecasting and shortage-risk components were integrated into the working BloodLine prototype and verified as part of the complete application workflow.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To study which time-series models suit blood-demand data better than the baseline and Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) built earlier, and to plan how they would be compared.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Reviewed the limits of the baseline and SES models: both forecast a flat level, so they cannot represent the weekly pattern in daily demand.
  • Studied SARIMA (seasonal ARIMA) and Prophet as the two options named in the proposal, including what the order terms (p, d, q) and the seasonal terms mean and why a seven-day season fits daily demand.
  • Compared the options on practical grounds: data needed, ease of fitting, interpretability, dependencies and how well each can be evaluated fairly against the existing models.
  • Planned the evaluation protocol: a chronological train/test split, no use of future data when forecasting, MAE and RMSE as the metrics, and the moving-average baseline as the reference every model must beat.
  • Outlined how the model would be kept replaceable, so a new model can be added without changing the API.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: A clear plan: add SARIMA as a third candidate next to the baseline and SES, and compare all three on the same chronological backtest.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To document the complete requirements of the BloodLine platform in a Software Requirements Specification so that design, implementation and testing can be checked against it.

docs.title: Work Done
docs.text:
• Contributed to the SRS (version 1.0) for BloodLine with the team, mainly the sections on demand forecasting (FR-FCST), shortage-risk detection (FR-RISK) and the synthetic demand data, which match my part of the implementation.
  • Described the six user classes (donors, hospital coordinators, inventory staff, blood-bank manager, medical staff, system administrator) and what each role may do.
  • Wrote numbered functional requirements grouped by feature: authentication (FR-AUTH), inventory (FR-INV), demand forecasting (FR-FCST), shortage risk (FR-RISK), donor matching (FR-MATCH), requests, screening, notifications, reports and regional view, donor portal and administration.
  • Specified the shortage-risk rule: shortfall = forecast demand - current stock; LOW if shortfall <= 0, MODERATE up to 25% of stock, HIGH above 25% or when stock is zero and demand is expected.
  • Specified the donor-compatibility table and the matching rules (compatible group, availability, consent, cooldown period).
  • Defined the data model (users, donors, blood banks, inventory, transactions, demand history, predictions, alerts, requests, screening records).
  • Added non-functional requirements (inventory update within 1 s, dashboard within 3 s and donor search within 2 s for up to 50 users), security requirements and business rules, such as final donor clearance by medical staff only and simulated data never being presented as real.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text: SRS version 1.0 was completed and added to the repository. It became the checklist for the later implementation and evaluation work.
